ready to be funded and that it recommended be deferred. The Minister overrode that.
Why? Because he knows, and New Zealanders know,  that with dairy payouts starting
with a three —as in $3 -something, which is a real possibility —too many farms will go
close to the wall or to the wall. To bail themselves out, under pressure from their banks,
21 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5173
they will take whatever cash they can get from whoever is bidding. You can bet your
bottom dollar that a lot of those people will be offshore bidders—

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: Oh, here we go. Give the man a whistle.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: No, this is colour -blind, and it is real, and if the
backbench members of the Government want to ignore it, they will be in Opposition
very shortly. New Zealanders do not want our land sold out from under us. It does not
matter whether it is going to Canberra or Cambodia —they do not want that to h appen.
Meanwhile, the system remains unfixed. Callaghan Innovation, which the Minister gave
a few extra dollars to, is still doling out money on automatic grant criteria for its growth
grants, which has seen it funding potential fraudsters, foreign-owned multinationals, and
polluters who have not had environment consents, and it even funded the Oracle
America’s Cup challenge, not Team New Zealand. Can you believe it? What a mess.
Even leaders in the sector, like the Government’s Chief Science Advisor, have
panned that Minister’s performance. The Chief Science Advisor says that the system is
too reactive, and Professor Hendy from Auckland University is saying that the bias is
towards the old economy. We need to be building a new economy, one where we have a
reasonably high level of investment in research and development; where we diversify
our economy; where we strengthen the smart stuff, not just the farm stuff that comes
raw; where we add value to our primary commodities; where we build on our primary
sector, just like Denmark does; where we strengthen our manufacturing and services
alongside primary agriculture so that we are adding value, information, and smarts; and
where we are known worldwide as the highest -quality, most environmentally
sustainable, most  traceable producer of fine food products anywhere in the world, so
that every housewife in Britain, India, or America who wants to buy safe, sound food
for their kids knows that when you buy from New Zealand, you buy quality. But we are
not there because the Government is racing to the bottom.
The Government does not get it. It thinks that by just reinforcing the old economy
and being nice to the foreign -owned banks, it will all come right. Well, Mr Joyce, it is
not coming right. It is falling in a hole, a nd you have only got to go around the regions
to have everybody tell you that. [ Bell rung] New Zealanders know the truth, and it is
not—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! Otherwise that becomes anoth er
call.
A party vote  was called for on the question,  That Vote Business, Science and
Innovation, Vote Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, Vote Labour Market, and Vote
Transport be agreed to.
Ayes 63
New Zealand National 59; Māori Party 2; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 56
New Zealand Labour 32; Green Party 12; New Zealand First 12.
Votes agreed to.
Education Sector

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Members, we now move to votes in the
education secto r—volume B.5, volume 2. The question is that Vote Education, Vote
Education Review Office, and Vote Tertiary Education stand part of the schedules.

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.role: Chairperson of the Education and Science Committee
items.text: Education
is a priority for the National Government because we understand that a key to growing a
stronger economy is a skilled, creative, and productive workforce. A high -quality
5174 Estimates Debate 21 Jul 2015
education is essential for such a w orkforce. That is why this Government has increased
the education budget year after year. Budget 2015 will take total spending on early
childhood, primary, and secondary education to a record $10.8 billion in 2015 -16.
Along with this increase of funding, t his Government has also spent a lot of time and
effort on encouraging participation, improving achievement rates, and also fostering
collaboration across the education sector.
To have a world -class education what we need is not just money, time, or effort but
also a vision, and here I would like to congratulate the Hon Hekia Parata. Clearly the
Hon Hekia Parata has a vision and has made it her mission to realise the vision. The
vision is that in New Zealand every young person in every school every day will get the
best possible education so that they can be successful.
To achieve that, this Government has set a series of education targets —for instance,
in 2016, 98 percent of children starting school will have participated in quality early
childhood education. In 2017, 85 percent of 18 -year-olds will have achieved National
Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) level 2 or an equivalent qualification.
We are on the right track to meeting those targets. The national early childhood
education participation rate is now over 96 percent, less than 2 percent short of the 98
percent target we have set for early childhood education participation by 2016. By 2014
over 81 percent of 18 -year-olds achieved at least NCEA level 2, less than 3 percent
short of the 85 percent target for 2017. The targets are important because we want to see
more kids starting earlier, staying longer, and leaving with better qualifications. Budget
2015 will consolidate what we have achieved with extra funding, such as an extra $74.9
million over 4 years to cover the cost of more children attending early childhood
education services than ever before.
What we need to realise our vision is not just funding but also modern concepts of
education. We have, therefore, challenged old assumptions and also developed new
approaches, tailoring what we do to match the needs of our kids. I once followed
Minister Parata to visit a school in Christchurch. It was an eye -opening experience.
What I saw was a completely new setting of the classroom environmen t and also a new
way of teaching, which was totally different from my understanding. Much of the new
school environment and also the new way of teaching is based on modern technology.
For instance, I did not see a blackboard or a whiteboard. What I saw was  a big screen in
the classroom. Modern technology means more investment in modern infrastructure for
schools. Budget 2015 commits a total of $373.9 million to improving our schools’
infrastructure over the next 4 years.
I would like, finally, to say a few words about tertiary education. First of all,
congratulations to the Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and Employment, the Hon
Steven Joyce, on the wonderful job he has done. Budget 2015 provides a further $112.3
million to boost tertiary education and skills. Thank you.
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): It is great to have the opportunity to follow the  Education and Science
Committee chair, Dr Jian Yang, and talk about this, as he says, very, very important part
of the Government’s work, which is growing the skills of young New Zealanders, in
particular, for the 21 st century economy. I am going to focus  my comments on the
tertiary education system, where the Government has been delivering very, very good
results in terms of increased numbers of full -time students, increased levels of study at
the higher levels, and increased numbers of graduates over the last 5 years on—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: What planet is the Minister on? Numbers are dropping.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: This Government has delivered far more while maintaining
its investment in tertiary education. The member opposite is now making the point that
21 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5175
numbers are starting to drop, which is, of course, correct. As the economy recovers
there are fewer people in full-time study.
But this Government has taken the decision to invest any money saved back into the
system in areas such as engineering, science, and so on, areas where we need further
investment to ensure we deliver the best possible results for our students. The whole
sector is working very hard on the tertiary education strategy, which runs from last year
through until 2019. That has half a dozen themes. I thought I would just cover them
very briefly because they are important.
The first one is delivering skills for industry. We have heard a lot of talk in this
Chamber tonight about the importance of diversifying our economy, which is absolutely
correct and it is exactly what this Government is doing. In order to do so, we need more
people with skills in engineering, in information and communications technology, in the
physical sciences, in the agricul tural sciences, and so on. That is exactly what we are
delivering with the increased investment in tuition subsidies in those areas. We have
also done a major reorganisation of the industry training system, which has streamlined
and increased the efficienc y of that system and is now delivering many more
tradespeople who are actually achieving qualifications rather than just being on the list
that the previous Government used to have. Those people are doing particularly well.
The second priority is getting a t-risk young people into a career. That is hugely
important. We have a number of initiatives in that space —obviously the Youth
Guarantee and trades academies. This Government has put more into this space than any
others. It is another of the areas where we  inherited a situation where there had been a
lot of hand -wringing but not a lot of action, and now there is very, very significant
action in this area.
We also have action in the Māori and Pasifika Trades Training Initiative, which is
the latest initiativ e. It also coincides with priority three, which is boosting the
achievement of Māori and Pasifika. The Māori and Pasifika Trades Training Initiative is
an innovative concept that in some ways is back to the future, in that it picks up the
young Māori cadetships that we had many, many years ago. It supplies whanau support.
In the case of Pasifika it supplies community and Pasifika church support. That is
getting a whole lot of younger people, in particular, into jobs, into industry training, and
into apprenticeship training.
The fourth priority is improving adult literacy and numeracy through the intensive
literacy and numeracy fundings and the workplace literacy and numeracy. We are going
through a process at the moment of assessing how those are going. We h ave increased
the amount in those areas. We have put a big emphasis on mainstreaming, if you like,
the literacy and numeracy at the lower levels of study. That has meant many, many
thousands of people have been properly assessed for literacy and numeracy t raining.
That work is ongoing in terms of providing second -chance learners the opportunity for
better skills of literacy and numeracy while they are in the workplace.
The fifth priority is strengthening research-based institutions. I understand there have
been some comments about the Performance -based Research Fund tonight. That has
been hugely important in investing and increasing science funding. This Government
has taken that from $250 million a year up to $300 million a year. The centres of
research excellence have gone from, I think, six to 10. So we are putting in some big
investments—things like the Marsden Fund, which is another portfolio but,
nevertheless, those are big investments. Our total science spend has gone from around
$780 million a year to  $1.5 billion. You will not hear that from the Opposition, but,
actually, that is what is going on.

items.speaker: Andrew Bayly
items.text: How much was that?
5176 Estimates Debate 21 Jul 2015

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Seven hundred and eighty million - odd dollars; then we
came up to abou t $1.5 billion in the 2015 -16 year. So those investments are very
important.

items.speaker: JENNY SALESA
items.text: This Government and its Budget
may use clever politics, but it has no plans to address our long -term challenges facing
New Zealand. It promised a Budget surplus and on Budget day it did not deliver on that
promise.
We believe that every New Zealander should be entitled to access quality public
education of the highest standard thr oughout their entire lives. Quality education
ensures that every Kiwi, regardless of who they are, where they come from, and
whether or not they are rich or poor, can achieve their full potential to contribute to our
society and our economy.
This Governmen t claims, as we have just heard from the Minister for Tertiary
Education, Skills and Employment, that changes to tertiary education are providing
results. It is great for people to get qualifications, and we expect to see constant changes
and improvements over the years in this particular area, but what we are also seeing is
universities and polytechnics being required to do so much more with much less money.
National has been underfunding the tertiary education sector for far too long, and the
cracks are beginning to show.
On Budget day it was announced —as we heard the chair of the Education and
Science Committee address before —that there is $130 million worth of operating
funding over the next 4 years for tertiary education. But when the tertiary education
Minister was questioned about this when he came to the select committee, he conceded
that only $7 million of this funding was actually new money. The rest of the balance
was made up of reallocations, and it is not new funding at all. That is not being str aight-
up with New Zealanders.
New Zealand now ranks close to the bottom of the OECD on tertiary education
spending per student. We are behind Australia, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France,
Germany, and a few other countries. We are well below the OECD averag e. Under this
Government the total spending on tertiary education has fallen from $3.194 billion in
2009 to $3 billion in 2015. We need further investment in tertiary education, not radical
restructuring to align our universities and our polytechnics with the Government’s
corporate view of the world in which it interferes with academic freedom, democracy,
and independence.
Under this Government we have around 70,000 young New Zealanders who are not
in employment, education, or training—or the “neet” numbers. This number is just way
too high. It is not acceptable. Under this Government, 40 percent of our total
unemployed are young people. Again, it is just unacceptable. This is the highest
percentage of total unemployment of any youth population whatsoever i n the OECD
countries. I do not know about you, Mr Chairperson, but I think that this statistic is
really quite shameful for a country like New Zealand. We have one of the best
educational systems in the world, and yet we have 40 percent of our total unempl oyed
being young people. This surely is something that must be addressed. This Government
is focused on the 1,600 or so 16 to 17-year-olds, but I think that this focus is wrong. The
focus should instead be on the 70,000 or so young people who are currently  not in
employment, education, or training.
The safety of our children should be paramount and it should be the main objective
when the Government considers funding for school buses, not cutting costs. So buried
in the details of this year’s Budget is $90 million worth of funding cuts for school
transport. We remember the horror ride for Green Bay High School students one
afternoon when they had a relief driver. The safety of our children when riding in school
21 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5177
buses should definitely not be one of those thi ngs that the Government looks at in terms
of cost-cutting. I do not know of any parent —not one—who would want their children
to experience or to go through a similar traumatic experience like the one that these
Green Bay students went through because of this Government’s cost-cutting measures.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chair. It was incredibly interesting
earlier today at question time to see the Hon Anne Tolley stand and talk about the 5 0-
millionth—or the 5 -millionth or whatever it was —breakfast that the National
Government is now taking credit for—

items.speaker: Andrew Bayly
items.text: Nine million over 5 years.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Whatever it is, she was taking 100 percent credit for it. But I
went to a breakfast meeting of principals when national standards was introduced and
the Hon Anne Tolley was the Minister of Education. Decile 1 and decile 2 principals
said “Minister, we cannot educate these children until they are fed and until  they are
clothed.”, and that Minister said: “Don’t give me your excuses —don’t give me your
excuses.” Yet today the same Minister, now in a different portfolio, is now taking credit
for the 5 -millionth—or whatever it was —breakfast and lauding the fact that  those
children—[Interruption]—no, wait, Mr Smith; wait, Mr Smith —are now having better
academic outcomes. It is unbelievable to see that today—unbelievable.
The other thing that was incredibly interesting just then was Mr Joyce standing up
and saying: “In this Budget, in education funding in these appropriations, we have got a
focus for students on 21st century education.” Not in Northland, apparently, according to
Hekia Parata —not in Northland. There is no digital aspiration there. There are no
lawyers, there are no accountants, there is no higher education, and there is no greater
reach for these students. Hekia Parata said —today—that the schools in Northland need
to be teaching those students how they can be forestry workers and fisheries operators
and how to work in tourism and marine manufacturing, because they need to have an
education that equips them only to go and be an employee in their local area for the
low-paid wages that those areas have.
Where is the aspiration, supposedly, out of this great 21st century economic drive
towards education? Not in Northland, apparently —not for these students. No, no, no,
no. Apparently in Northland, apart from the fact that you can travel on roads that
nobody is going to fix up, at the same time the Government is  going to give you just
enough education so that you can go and get a job on a fishing boat. There is nothing
wrong with getting a job on a fishing boat, but where is the aspiration from this
Government for Northland? Not in this Budget—not in these appropriations.
I will tell you something else that is very interesting. This Government has an
underspend—and again, that member over there said: “Wait for another month to get a
surplus.” Wait for another month to get a surplus —they certainly will. There is $2 05
million worth of underspend in education from this Government. Why? Because it is
desperate to get a surplus. It is desperate to get a surplus, and it is going to short -change
special needs children across this country—

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: That’s not true.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: —special needs children across this country. There is a zero
Budget for gifted and talented children, Mr Foster -Bell—a zero Budget for gifted and
talented children who are in the spectrum of special needs, but you can get it if you have
got behavioural problems. According to this Government, if you have got behavioural
problems—if you are gifted but you are naughty —the Ministry of Education will give
you some money. It will give you some money. But if you are gifted and need to be
extended or need to have programmes like the One Day School or other programmes
such as that, there is a zero Budget in here, and who removed it? Who removed the
Budget spend that was there? The National Government. Who took away “well above”
5178 Estimates Debate 21 Jul 2015
national standards? The National Government. So, you see, it is very interesting for
National members to stand up and say that they invest in education.
Here is another thing that they invest in. They talk about the international student
body, they talk about these new information and communications technology schools,
and so on and so forth. I went to a private training establishment provider the other day.
This Government has capped domestic hospitality and chef students at 300 only, inside
that organisation, but there are 600 international students. It is a growth industry for this
country and there is a skills shortage throughout the world, and yet this Government
caps domestic students. This Government will not put a budget around domestic
students but will allow international students en masse into this country to subsidise the
education that it should be providing for New Zealanders.
There are 70,000 students who are not in education, employment, or training —
“neets”—and there were 70,000 i nternational work visas given out in the last year.
There are 70,000 New Zealand students who are “neets” and 70,000 international
students who got work visas in the last year from this Government. This Government
does not invest in its own people, this Go vernment does not invest in its education, and
this Government has no aspiration for these young people unless you are in an urban
area, and then you can get not only some sort of spend; you can get a road to it.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak.
That speech from Tracey Martin was a load of rubbish. I normally rate that member
very highly, but the facts are these: under our Governme nt for the last 6 years we have
successively increased the education budget —$10.8 billion in the most difficult
financial times. Every single year we have increased the education budget. Secondly,
when it comes to our most vulnerable students, whether that  is students who have
special education difficulties or whether that is those students who have had real issues
in terms of numeracy and literacy, this Budget is better than ever for them.
Let us walk through it. If we look at early childhood education par ticipation,
particularly around Māori and Pacific young people, that is up. That is up by 4 to 5
percent. That is incredibly significant, and that is about the future of our country. When
we actually look at the facts in terms of participation around early  childhood education,
we are absolutely on track for 98 percent. We have got more money going into early
childhood education—I think there is $75 million in this Budget. That is about doing
everything we can to make sure that all students in this country are successful.
When it comes to special education, this Budget is great in terms of special
education. We have got $40 million going into ongoing resourcing scheme funding.
That means that for the 500 young people who have and need that additional support,
whether that is teacher -aide time, whether that is physiotherapy, or whether that is
speech language therapy, we are putting the resource into them.
I want to acknowledge the Hon Hekia Parata. I think this is a great Budget in terms
of what she has done. She has real vision, and she is investing in some of our most
vulnerable students. The Budget also includes $24 million for additional class support.
That is 1,500 —that is the first phase of another group of students who need that
additional help in terms of our education system. So when that member tells us that
somehow we have underfunded education, well, it is a 26 percent increase in special
education. Under our Government there is $500 million more for some of our most
vulnerable students.
When it come s to trade academies there is more money than ever. So when that
member says that we are not aspirational for Northland, that is a complete load of
rubbish. What are we doing in terms of modern learning and education environments
for Northland? Well, the o ther day I found out that we are so far ahead of schedule in
terms of the roll out of Network for Learning —that is fast, uncapped data paid for by
21 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5179
the Crown; a real passport to the future for these students —that 600,000 students are
now connected. That is students in Northland. That is a Government that is aspirational
for those people in Northland. That is real, actual resources going to those students in
Northland. That is on the back of $700 million of investment in both ultra -fast
broadband and uncapped data, ensuring that our students are equipped for the future.
When it comes to school property, over 60 percent of our schools were more than 40
years old: we had leaky buildings, we had a whole range of design issues, and we had a
whole lot of relocatabl es. What have we done? We have invested billions of dollars in
terms of upgrading these schools and major redevelopments. I can confirm in this
Budget that we have got hundreds of millions of dollars as well going not only into new
schools but also into en suring that we can fix some of those really old schools. Today I
announced Lepperton School in North Taranaki. We have 14 schools through our major
redevelopment programme, we have got more coming, and this is on the back of
hundreds of millions of dollars as well in terms of investing in growth.
So in places like Auckland, Hamilton, and Queenstown this Budget is good because
we are actually building those schools and we are putting those classrooms where they
need to be, and we are doing that ahead of the curve. From my perspective we are
investing more than ever in both school property and modern learning environments,
but we are actually doing so much for vulnerable students. So we are a Government that
is not only aspirational and focused on the future f or those students but absolutely
focused on some of our most vulnerable students. That is crystal clear in this Budget
through the increase in terms of special education funding, through the increase in early
childhood participation funding, and through a range of other projects from the gateway
assessment programme, which is about ensuring that 3,800 needy children get access to
early childhood and schooling services, to the Year 9 Plus trial, which allocates $2.2
million to educational champions.
We are a  Government that has a strong social conscience and that is also very
focused on the economy. To hear from members opposite that we are not aspirational
about students and that we are not investing in them is an absolute load of rubbish. This
Government has successively increased the education budget every year since we have
been in Government.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Chair. Kia ora tātou katoa. It
is great to take a call on education because I do not believe that there is anyone in the
Education and Science Committee who is not interested and concerned about aspects of
education. Often members of the publ ic say to us: why do you not all put aside your
differences and just work together? But I think, listening to the debate tonight, there are
some underlying themes that make it clear why we do not always agree. One of those is
the pedagogical vision of what education is for, and I think we have heard very strongly
from the Government that it is aspirational, in its terms, for education and that the
purpose of education is to serve the economy.
That is not the view of the Green Party. The Green Party believes  that education is a
whole lot more than serving the economy and that, in fact, the economy should serve its
people. Education is about lifelong learning for all people, and it is not about —with due
respect to the chair of the Education and Science Committ ee, Dr Jian Yang —getting
them into education earlier for longer. It is actually about acknowledging that education
needs to be of quality and that the goal of education is equity. That is a very different
pedagogical goal, and that is why we have problems with the Government’s obsession
with targets and assessment, which is an educational model that is reductionist and
unsuccessful in other countries.
The current education estimates and the Minister at the select committee were all
about targets, targets, t argets. Why is that a problem? It is a problem because the early
5180 Estimates Debate 21 Jul 2015
childhood education sector may be about to reach 96 percent to 98 percent participation,
but when I asked the chief executive of the ministry about quality, he said: “That will
come later. We are going to get participation first and then we will find a way to figure
out how to improve quality.” So what in fact we have got is a huge push, including
through the Work and Income system, to make parents place their children under the
age of 5 into early childhood education, but quality has not yet been sorted out, people.
So how comfortable do we feel about making sure that our little children are all getting
this brilliant start in life, when there is no commitment to quality?
Therefore, we have go t the whole spectrum in early childhood education from the
absolutely inspiring and wonderful—often smaller in number, high -ratio trained teacher
centres plus the kōhanga and playcentre, where they have succeeded in holding on to
fantastic whānau engagement, which is increasingly hard in this economy—and then we
have got the opposite, which are basically baby barns, where people who do not have a
choice because they have no public transport and no resources are forced to use the
baby barn down the road, the  large franchise, the commercial model. So the education
sector is torn between a genuine commitment to learning, because it enhances our
humanity as well as our society as well as our economy, and making sure we meet
targets.
This Government has pushed th is right through to national standards and through to
the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA). So national standards —
again, another one of those measurables that actually does not deal with the
unmeasurable, which is children, because ch ildren all learn at different rates. We have
this system with NCEA as well, where we are claiming we are going to get to the target
of 80 percent achieving level 2, but again questions are being asked by academics about
whether we have lowered standards in  order to meet the target; what the real quality is
of what is happening in our secondary schools.
So if we are concerned about public quality education, it is not enough to spout the
numbers and talk the rhetoric. It is absolutely not enough. We actually have to know
whether early childhood education is of quality, because the most important years that
we pay lip service to are our small children. We have to know that kids are getting lunch
as well as breakfast, which is where the Green Party has stood str ong on feeding
children properly, and not saying that if charities and the Government want to have a bit
of a partnership and have breakfast, that is OK; they do not need lunch. Well, of course
if we lifted wages and had a decent economy, then the parents could afford it, but right
now, as was shown in the House today in our question on inequality, we have a long
way to go on that, so we still need to feed our children in schools. That is why we need
a decent school lunch programme.
Honestly, there are some inspiring programmes that schools are leading, but they are
paying for it themselves in many instances. Sometimes teachers are paying for it,
sometimes communities have stepped up, but there is no consistency and there is a real
need for a decent, State -supported lunch programme that is flexible and school and
community-led.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a second
brief call in this debate and to focu s on education issues, where once again we see that
we have a Government that is long on promises, long on rhetoric, and not delivering in
the reality. Let us take members opposite at their word. I think all parents care for
nothing more than the well -being of their children, and I believe members opposite are
sincere in their wish to see our children succeed. The question is whether the
programme that they are enacting is going to deliver on that promise.
Let us first look at the compulsory education secto r and then at the tertiary sector.
The Government has been known for two great changes to compulsory education:
21 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5181
national standards and charter schools. National standards have been panned around the
world. They cause people to teach to the test. They are t he exact opposite of what a
modern millennial economy demands, which is that you can get basic education off the
internet but you need to learn to think critically. That is why teaching to the test —one-
size-fits-all, absolute achievement rather than relati ve improvement —is a road to
pedagogical nowhere. In my electorate, where 40 percent of my constituents were not
born in New Zealand —and for many, many students English is not a first language —
having an English -based national standards, even if it were obje ctive, even if it were
specific, even if it were moderated objectively, which it is not, would make no sense at
all. The Government is taking education backwards.
The second great proposal of this Government is charter schools, and charter schools
make no sense. More money is given per student by miles, but the school does not have
to teach the curriculum, the teachers do not have to be licensed, they are not subject to
the Official Information Act, and in many cases the contracts the Government has
entered into are so brain -dead that the assets are not even secured. For example, a
Whangarei charter school has $2.5 million in taxpayer funding unaccounted for.
Another Auckland charter school was guaranteed funding for 160 places but maxed out
at 120 with, as far as I am aware, no recovery. More and more costs are being passed to
parents, and too many parents cannot afford them because of the rapidly growing
inequalities in our society. If a kid is hungry he or she cannot learn. Let us feed our kids,
let us give them a decent start, and let us have an education system that actually teaches
what kids are going to need in this 21st century.
Then we go on to tertiary education, and here once again the Government is, sadly,
not being straight with New Zealanders. Fr om the Minister’s own lips, as recorded in
the report of the Education and Science Committee, there was no $113 million “further
funding” for education. By the Minister’s own admission there was only $7 million, and
that is gross of an increased tax take f rom the Inland Revenue Department, which
actually makes it negative. But even if it were $7 million, that is a massive real -terms
cut to tertiary education. The tertiary system is underfunded. It has a micro -managing
Minister who lacks the credibility to get the funding, and he lacks the plan to deliver it.
The institutions in this sector are a mess. This Government removed the strategy and
policy function from the Tertiary Education Commission. It now says it just
operationalises things. Where has the stra tegy function gone? It is not found in the
Ministry of Education—it is focused on the compulsory sector. In reality, what there is
sits in the Ministry of —wait for it —Business, Innovation and Employment. That is, as
others have said, a reductionist view of  education and one that is patently not working.
For the individual student, pathways are not there to the jobs of the future. Why not?
Because the funding cuts are biting.
The Government has put an arbitrary 7 -year limit on student loans —the famous “7
EFTS” policy, which means that even 40 percent of medical students cannot get funding
for their last 1 or 2 years of study. For other recognised long degrees —double degrees
or doctoral courses—the loans run out before the degree is awarded. That might be fine
if you are a silver spoon brigade kid, but if you are an average kid from an average
family, our country and you will be the poorer.

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER-BELL
items.text: It is a rather intimidating p rospect to follow on
from that very learned and literate member, one of the most distinguished alumni of not
only Otago University, my old university, but also Harvard. Mr Cunliffe is a very
literate man. Does he love words? Yes, he does. Does he love the sound of his voice
saying those words? Absolutely. But we here tonight are talking about Vote Education
in this appropriations debate. I think that this Government is doing an excellent job in
improving the educational standards offered in the New Zealand public system.
5182 Estimates Debate 21 Jul 2015
Mr Cunliffe asked a couple of rhetorical questions in his contribution this evening. I
will concede that he gave us the benefit of the doubt in thinking that we were motivated
from a position of taking the best interests of New Zealand’s le arners, children and
students to heart, and that is the case, I can assure Mr Cunliffe. But he did raise the
question as to whether our policies would implement the goals of achieving what we set
out to achieve, and I think the added investment made in Bud get 2015 in the education
vote will go a long way towards providing better services and better outcomes for New
Zealand learners. Take, for instance, the $244 million for new classrooms and schools—
that is seven new schools, four major expansions of existi ng schools, and over 240 new
classrooms for New Zealand schools. This will provide modern learning spaces for
children in the New Zealand compulsory system.
I am particularly proud of the extra $62.9 million that my colleague Minister Nikki

items.speaker: Kaye referred to. This is for special education
items.text: those children who have the highest
needs and are the most vulnerable. This will include services such as additional teacher
aide support and the provision of speech and language therapy to those children who
need that little bit of extra help to be able to achieve and succeed. I am pleased to see an
extra $42.3 million going into school operational grants in order to help the smooth
running of our local schools.
The question that I guess we could also ask is: what do peo ple in this system actually
think of this? Well, I want to quote from a message I recently received. It is an email
and, unlike the Opposition, I am not going to name the gentleman, but I can assure them
that he is not Gene Simmons and he is not John Kerwin, who was also referenced by the
Opposition this evening. This is a real person —a staff member at the New Zealand Post
Primary Teachers Association. I do not want to quote it in full, because, well, I am a
humble person—he is very complimentary. But he go es on to say: “Minister Parata has
been great recently with her support for teachers, and I am really pleased to see it’s a
message that others in the National caucus are taking to heart. You also showed a really
good understanding of the educational succe ss programme, which, as you know, the
PPTA supports. It’s a pity that there are still people mistakenly characterising it as some
form of competitive performance pay, which has meant that we’ve taken flak from some
of our more usual allies.” I presume that  they are referring to the Labour Party and the
Greens.
So the post -primary teaching profession is in support of our programme, which
implements our targets of achieving 98 percent of early childhood education enrolment;
particularly around the 85 percent of 18-year-olds who we want to graduate with NCEA
level 2—that is the equivalent of the old Sixth Form Certificate —and also our target of
eventually getting 60 percent of all 25 to 34 -year-olds accredited with an NCEA level 4
qualification. That is a post-compulsory qualification.
In the local context here in Wellington, we are going to see a new information and
communications technology graduate school added to the existing high -quality tertiary
institutions we have: Victoria University, Massey Universit y, WelTec, Whitireia
Community Polytechnic, and other private training establishments such as the Campbell
Institute, which brings valuable export education dollars into Wellington and provides a
useful experience both to those international students who c ome here and to the New
Zealand students who are exposed to the opportunities of having colleagues who come
from China, from Viet Nam, from Japan, from Europe—in fact, from all over the world.
This Government is doing a lot in the education sector. There i s a lot to be proud of.
There is work remaining to do, and the feedback that I am getting, both in the
Wellington Central electorate and around New Zealand as we visit on Education and
Science Committee visits, is wholly positive about the efforts this Gov ernment is
making.
21 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5183

Environment Sector

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Members, we now come to votes in the
environment sector —volume B.5, volume 3. The question is that Vote Conservation,
Vote Environment, and Vote Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment stand
part of the schedules.
Scott Simpson (Chai rperson of the Local Government and Environment
Committee): It is a great pleasure to stand and rise to speak in the Committee stage of
the Appropriation (2015/16 Estimates) Bill. I chair the Local Government and
Environment Committee, and it was a great pleasure to have before the committee at the
estimates hearings only a few weeks ago three of the most competent, most able, most
inspired, and most passionate advocates for our environment, and they all happen to be
Cabinet Ministers in this John Key National-led Government.
We had before the committee the Minister of Conservation, the Hon Maggie Barry,
who has spent an entire life working in the area of conservation and is dedicated to
preserving our natural environment in a way that most New Zealanders un derstand
completely because they have seen her for years on our screens. She has a reputation
and a credible track record that is unimpeachable in terms of her commitment to our
environment and to conservation in New Zealand.
We had before us the Minister  for the Environment, the Hon Nick Smith. He is
another person who has dedicated his life and his parliamentary political career to
ensuring that the New Zealand environment and the standards we have as a nation are
constantly improved. We had before us also the Minister for Climate Change Issues, the
Hon Tim Groser, who has brought to that portfolio a level of intellectual rigour that was
never apparent when other Governments occupied the Treasury benches.
Those three Cabinet Ministers provided the Local Government and Environment
Committee with a very good understanding and analysis of what is essentially this
Government’s blue-green agenda for our environment. It is a blue -green agenda that is
based on the principles of economic growth and improving the environment hand in
hand, at the same time. They are not mutually exclusive. Those principles include an
absolute understanding that good science is critical to quality environmental decision -
making at every level, and, further, that collaborative solution s developed by sectors
and communities working together are far more sustainable and enduring than any kind
of policy rant and cant that can occur from members opposite.
There are six priority areas that the Minister has presented to the select committee
and they made it clear that resource management reform is still an absolute high priority
on this Government’s agenda. I am confident from the messages that we saw—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I am sor ry to interrupt the honourable
member. The time has come for me to report progress.
Progress reported.
Report adopted.
The House adjourned at 9.56 p.m.

TUESDAY, 21 JULY 2015 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
VISITORS 
Australia—Delegation, Victorian Legislative Assembly 
Mr SPEAKER : Honourable members, I am sure that members would wish to 
welcome a delegation from the Victorian Legislative Assembly, led by the Hon 
Matthew Guy, Leader of the Opposition, who are present in the gallery. 
AUTHORITY TO ADMINISTER OATH 
Mr SPEAKER: Members, the following authorisations have been received by the 
Deputy Speaker and the Clerk of the House from His Excellency the Governor-General 
to administer the oath or affirmation prescribed by law to be taken or made by members 
of the House. The authorisations read: 
Pursuant to section 11 of the Constitution Act 1986, I, Lieutenant General The Right 
Honourable Si r Jerry Mateparae, Governor -General of New Zealand, hereby authorise 
you, 
The Honourable Kerry James (Chester) Borrows 
Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives 
and 
David Martin Wilson 
Clerk of the House of Representatives 
to administer to members of Parliament the Oath or Affirmation of Allegiance to Her 
Majesty The Queen required to be taken or made by every such member before that 
member shall be permitted to sit or vote in the House of Representatives.  
BILL ENGLISH, Acting Prime Minister 
Authorised 
Jerry Mateparae, Governor-General 
16 July 2015 
ORAL QUESTIONS 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Housing Market—Foreign Ownership of New Zealand Properties 
1. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Does 
he stand by all his statements? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: Does he stand by his statement in 2010 that “Looking four, 
five, ten years into the future I’d hate to see New Zealanders as tenants in their own 
country …”; if so, why, after almost 7 years, has his Government failed to collect 
specific information on foreign buying of land and homes in New Zealand? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: In answer to the first part of the question, yes.  
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Is he aware that both Beijing and Shanghai, for example, 
have laws preventing non -residents from inflating demand and buying houses in those 
cities, and does he consider that such measures would be racist if applied here? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Well, every country has different rules, but what I would say 
is the current rules around foreign investment were actually passed by the Labour 
5104 Oral Questions 21 Jul 2015 
 
Government in 2005. They are actually in line with the vast majority of developed 
countries. For example, in t he UK, the US, Canada, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, 
Japan, Sweden, and many other OECD countries, there are no or very few restrictions 
on foreigners buying residential property. When it comes to Australia, which, 
theoretically, has a restriction in re lation to second -hand properties, it has been 
spectacularly unsuccessful.  
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Why will his Government not, in his own words, “get 
some guts” and introduce restrictions on foreign buyers of our homes and land, like , for 
example, in China, Hong Kong, and Singapore, or are they too racist and xenophobic? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Well, for a start, I am proud to lead a Government where if we 
were to make changes around foreign investment, it would be to every  country and 
every ethnicity, and we would not just cook things up and single people out.  
Rt Hon Winston Peters: Is it not the case that his opposition to New Zealand First’s 
foreign ownership of land and homes register bill is because he is scared of Kiwis 
finding out under his watch just how much land and housing have been flogged off to 
overseas buyers? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: No, in our view it was poorly drafted.  
Economy—International Conditions and Performance 
2. CHRIS BISHOP (National)  to the Minister of Finance : What reports has he 
received on the international economy, and its effect on the New Zealand economy? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : I have seen a number of reports, 
including Treasury’s Monthly Economic Indicators . As members will be aware, there 
have been continued drops in the international dairy price recently. It is now  40 percent 
lower than the recent peak in early March. For the dairy sector, times are turning out to 
be tougher, and they may be for longer, than industry experts expected. However, New 
Zealand’s automatic stabilisers, in the form of flat to falling interest rates and a reducing 
exchange rate against the US and Australian dollar, will help cushion the effects of a 
dairy price decline and increase the profits of other export sectors, where prices are 
holding up.  
Chris Bishop: What matters of economic relevance for New Zealand did he observe 
on his recent visit to China?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH : Both political leaders and business operators in China 
remain reasonably positive about the economic outlook. China’s growth does appear t o 
be slowing, more so probably in investment in infrastructure than in consumer demand, 
where rising wages and a continued demand for high -quality food products would tend 
to underpin more growth in New Zealand rather than less. It is good news for New 
Zealand to see China officially moving from an investment -driven economy to more 
emphasis on consumption driving growth.  
Chris Bishop : How does New Zealand’s current economic performance compare 
with other developed economies?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH : New Zealand faces some of the same headwinds as other 
developed economies—2.6 percent GDP growth in the year to March compares with an 
average of about 2 percent growth across the OECD. Tourism, for instance, is growing 
reasonably strongly because the New Zealand dollar has dropped relative to the US 
dollar, and this last year we have had 3 million visitors, a 7 percent increase on the 
previous year, indicating there is sufficient economic growth and confidence in other 
developed economies to supply more tourists to New Zealand.  
Chris Bishop : How well placed is the New Zealand economy to deal with any 
potential slow -down in the rate of economic growth should international conditions 
worsen?  
21 Jul 2015 Oral Questions 5105 
 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: In the light of recent commentary on the economy, that is a 
very good question. The Reserve Bank’s latest forecast, just 6 weeks ago, incorporated 
reductions in dairy prices and at the same time forecast growth of over 3 percent in the 
next few years. Recent data indicates that those forecasts may come back a little, but we 
remain on track for sustained moderate growth. As I have indicated, the exchange rate 
has dropped considerably, cushioning the effect of lower dairy prices, and interest rate s 
are now flat to falling, rather than rising as was expected just 3 or 4 months ago. That 
will help households that may face some headwinds from lower dairy prices.  
Housing Market—Auckland and Foreign Ownership of New Zealand Properties 
3. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by his statement in relation to affordability of homes in Auckland that “there’s a 
general view that housing prices are not overvalued”, given that the homeownership rate 
has fallen to its lowest level in 64 years? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : This is a very misleading piece of selective 
quoting, and in fact was not made in relation to the affordability of homes in Auckland 
at all. I stand by the full statement I made. When asked to comment on the fact that New 
Zealand has not had a housing correction in 45 years, I said “One of the reasons why 
you pr obably haven’t had a significant correction is because over the last 45 years 
there’s probably been a general view that houses are not overvalued relative to a whole 
lot of different factors. My point is that the market, in the end, assesses when housing i s 
massively overvalued compared to fundamentals, not politicians.” 
Andrew Little: Does he still think that the typical Auckland house is affordable for 
the typical Auckland family, when prices have risen five times faster than incomes 
under his watch and the median house now costs 10 times the median household 
income?  
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: There are a variety of different measures around affordability, 
but what I do know is that house prices doubled under the previous Labour 
Government, and interest rates are considerably lower than they were under the 
previous Labour Government. If one even looks at homeownership rates, our 
homeownership rate, at 64.8 percent, is highly comparable with other OECD countries. 
Andrew Little : Is he aware that in the past year the number of owner -occupied 
homes fell by 2,400 while the number of rentals rose by 19,800, and does that not show 
that his policies are favouring investors while taking the Kiwi dream of homeownership 
away from families? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : No. There are a variety of different reasons why people may 
move into rental properties. For one thing, Auckland actually has been growing in size, 
and many people move to a city and rent a property as the starting thing that they do. 
Andrew Little : Why is it the policy of this Government —of his Government —to 
allow overseas speculators to profit off New Zealand homes, contributing nothing to our 
economy while pushing prices out of the reach of more and more families? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Firstly, I reject that, but, secondly, we have the policies that 
were introduced, actually, by the Labour Government. It passed the foreign investment 
rules in 2005. Apparently, Winston was part o f it, happily praising it and voting for it. 
They were good enough for Labour in Government, but they are not good enough for 
Labour in Opposition. Mind you, it is a very different Labour Party these days, is it not? 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I am calling for less interjection from 
my right-hand side. 
Andrew Little: Can he guarantee that the Inland Revenue Department database will 
be public and will clearly reveal the number of non -residents buying New Zealand 
houses? 
5106 Oral Questions 21 Jul 2015 
 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : As the member knows, there is a process that we are going 
through at the moment. There is a bill in the House, and we will be looking at that data. 
But what I do know is our information will not be cooked up, and when  someone asks 
me a question about it I will not lose my rag at TV3 like that member did before. 
Andrew Little : Why did he give offshore speculators 4 -months’ notice of the 
upcoming change of rules, giving them time to game the old system, w hen he cancelled 
the KiwiSaver kick -start on the day of the Budget so that parents could not sign their 
kids up? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: If the member ever gets into Government, then he may realise 
that tax law is a very complicated and complex thing. If we had not actually had a 
period of time where there was an opportunity for tax specialists and others to give 
input into the process, then you may have got unintended consequences. Secondly, 
nothing changes under tax law in New Zealand as a resu lt of the brightline test. If 
someone buys on revenue account then they will still be subject to paying tax. You can 
be sure, as I said at my post -Cabinet press conference yesterday afternoon, that the 
Inland Revenue Department will be looking very closely  at people who buy houses at 
the moment, like it does all the time, and it will be collecting tax revenue off people 
who owe it. 
Andrew Little: If he has done all he can on housing why are Auckland house prices 
accelerating rather than stabilising, why are the number of homes owned by people who 
live in them falling, and why are so many offshore websites urging speculators to keep 
on buying in Auckland? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : As we know, we really have to question any piece of da ta or 
information the Labour Party puts out there these days in whatever language it 
introduces it. I actually stand by the Government’s record on what we have done: 118 
special housing areas, on which we expect 50,000 new dwellings, the vast bulk of which 
are in Auckland; the brightline test that is there; the $50 million that is set aside for 
residential housing development; the KiwiSaver HomeStart programme, which, as I saw 
the other day in the paper, is doing exceedingly well; and the other rules that w e have 
changed around the cost of imported materials. This Government has done a great deal 
when it comes to housing— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The answer is quite long enough. 
Prime Minister—Flag Referendum and Climate Change 
4. JAMES SHAW (Co -Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he stand by 
his statement that “I’d bet my bottom dollar that there would be considerable debate and 
discussion in New Zealand about whether the flag should change”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : Yes, I do. I made that comment when the 
flag consideration project had received about 2,300 different flag designs. I am 
delighted to inform the member that at the last count the panel had received 10,291 flag 
designs. My bottom dollar is pretty safe, I think. 
James Shaw: Does he accept that only 25 percent of New Zealanders want to change 
the flag, whereas 87 percent of New Zealanders are concerned about climate change? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: No, I do not think you actually can make that prediction until 
we go through the referendum process. As the member knows, there will be two 
referenda in relation to the flag change. I think we are ultimately going to have to wait 
until that final referendum takes place in early 2016 to see whether New Zealanders 
want to change the flag or not. I hope they do, because I believe passionately that a new 
flag can be used as part of a way of  showing how proud we are of our country and of 
how we unify a multicultural society. 
21 Jul 2015 Oral Questions 5107 
 
James Shaw: Given that climate change submissions outnumbered flag submissions 
by 15,000 to 2,300, does he think that changing the flag was the right priorit y for him to 
personally champion? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Well, I would say —and I have said this on numerous 
occasions—that the flag is just one of a great many issues as Prime Minister that I have 
a hand on. I have never argued that it is the m ost important one. In fact, back in 2010 
when that issue was raised significantly with me, I made the point there that there were 
much bigger and more important issues to deal with at the time. But over time I think 
we can actually consider a whole range o f different factors. When it comes to climate 
change, the member is right. There were 17,023 submissions received by the 
Government, but, actually, most of those were stock standard ones. They were pro 
forma and they were prompted by the Green Party. In fa ct, there were only 1,485 
submissions that were unique. If we go to the flag—something of interest because it was 
the member’s primary question—he may be interested to know that there were 146,000 
views of the New Zealand flag history video, that 6,000 peo ple visited workshops and 
information stands, and that there were more than 850,000 online visits and about 2.7 
million views of the flag gallery. I need to tell the member that every single night when 
I am in my office, I am signing letters thanking the y oung people of New Zealand who 
are writing to me, I have got to say, in their hundreds— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Now I have heard enough. 
James Shaw: I thank the Prime Minister for his acknowledgment of how successful 
the Green Party was at galvanising public opinion. 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Just ask the supplementary question. 
James Shaw : If he plans to listen to the public on changing the flag, why did his 
Government not listen to the 99 percent of submitters who arg ued for a 2030 emissions 
reduction target of at least 40 percent below 1990 levels? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Because, in the end, of course we undertake consultation, but 
consultation does not always mean agreement with a specific point of view. The target 
that we have come up with —minus 30 percent off a 2005 base —we believe, is actually 
a balanced and fair target to take in. It is just one of the things that we do think is about 
right, given the cost to our economy and the challenges that we have  with half of our 
emissions coming from agriculture. The other point that we have made with the target is 
that we are quite happy to increase that target over time, if we can get some of the 
scientific solutions we need for agriculture. I am actually very confident, as I am sure 
the member himself will be, that over the next 10 to 15 years there will be a significant 
breakthrough when it comes to agriculture. 
Andrew Little : In light of the increase in economic hardship, especially in the 
regions, does he now accept that there are better uses for $26 million of taxpayers’ 
money than a flag referendum that the public does not want? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Well, firstly, we do not know what the final cost of the 
referendum process wil l be. I simply say that because Labour and the Greens actually 
pushed along a referendum on the mixed -ownership model after we had had a general 
election that we won with a landslide on this very topic. In the end, the estimates were 
$9 million and the act ual costs were $6.7 million. But here is the point: this is a major 
constitutional issue, and this party believes in democracy in the same way that this party 
believes in a multicultural society and being fair and decent to people and not cooking 
things up. That is what the National— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
James Shaw: Given his answer about costs to the New Zealand economy of strong 
action on climate change, would he say that the majority of the 520 businesses surveyed 
by Waikato University were wrong to think that when it comes to climate change 
5108 Oral Questions 21 Jul 2015 
 
“There is a risk that weak Government inaction will still incur most of the costs without 
capturing the potential benefits.”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Well, I did not see the sur vey and I do not know the 
companies that have been asked the question. I do not think that that is actually right, 
though, because if we look at the emissions trading scheme, that, in fact, actually sheets, 
ultimately, the costs home to businesses that nee d to change their practices —but, 
ultimately, those businesses will pass those costs on to consumers —or they go directly 
to consumers. The issue we have got here is that we get about 80 percent of our energy 
from renewable sources. We have about half of our  emissions coming from agriculture, 
and the Treasury advice to the Government, as I recall it, was that the cost of our 
making the sorts of reductions that, say, for instance, the European Union promised are 
much, much higher in this country. I think we ha ve just got to get that balance about 
fair, and I think we have. This is just one of the varied tools that we are using around 
climate change. There will be others over time. I accept, actually, that it is an important 
issue. The Government is taking it seriously. 
James Shaw: So if he does not believe that those businesses were correct, or that the 
99 percent of submitters were correct, does he also believe that the 24 percent of 
National Party voters polled by UMR who think that New Zealand sh ould take stronger 
action on climate change are also wrong? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I did not say that the member was wrong and that those 
businesses were wrong. I was quite clear when I said that I did not see the survey and I 
do not know the particular companies that it asked. Each will have a different 
perspective. But there are hundreds of thousands of companies, I suspect, in New 
Zealand; the 500 are just a snapshot of what is there. I accept the view, actually, that 
climate change is an im portant issue, and I accept the view that New Zealand needs to 
do its fair share, and I accept the view that there is a strong case that New Zealand 
might, over time, be able to do more. But I am just simply making the point that if we 
ask our farmers to d o that and we cannot give them any scientific solutions, we are 
simply putting a cost on them without their being able to actually change their 
behaviour. That is just called a tax, and I do not think that actually helps the consumers 
of the world who will have to pay for those products. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: Can he confirm that only one party, when asked by him to 
join the cross-party parliamentary committee on his flag change, would not join, and it 
told him that it was a $26 milli on waste of taxpayers’ money and to shove his Benedict 
Arnold idea where the sun does not shine? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Well, I do not recall the letter saying to shove it where the sun 
don’t shine, but I do remember the dinosaurs party saying that it did not want to take 
part. 
James Shaw : Given the strong public preference for greater action on climate 
change than on flag change, is he willing to work with other political parties to come up 
with a more ambitious emissions reduction target? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : No, the Government has got its position when it comes to 
climate change targets. It is quite a legitimate thing for every political party to have its 
own target and its own set of policies, but we take those to a general election. 
B4 School Checks—Reports 
5. SIMON O’CONNOR (National —Tāmaki) to the Minister of Health : What 
recent reports has he received on the number of B4 School free health and development  
checks completed in the last financial year, and what do they show? 
21 Jul 2015 Oral Questions 5109 
 
Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN (Minister of Health) : I have received a report 
that 58,600 children received B4 School Checks in primary care in the year to June, and 
that this is a record 92 percent of eligible children. B4 School Checks test a child’s 
hearing, vision, and oral health. Behaviour, developmen t, and growth are all assessed, 
and immunisations are also checked. The Government invests $10 million each year to 
provide these free primary care B4 School Checks, which have now benefited more than 
300,000 children and which ensure that Kiwi kids start school in the best possible 
health. 
Simon O’Connor: Has he had to do any checking of the numbers in recent reports 
relating to checks on children? 
Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN : Yes, I have. My office had to spend a lot  of 
time last week following up a claim that 22 out of 26 GP practices in central Auckland 
had opted out of free visits for under -13s, but several hours later the Labour Party 
apologised to journalists, conceding that their figures— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The Minister will resume his seat. 
Chris Hipkins: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I have two points of order, Mr 
Speaker.  
Mr SPEAKER: I will have the first one. 
Chris Hipkins : The first one is that it is actually a real stretch to get the 
supplementary question related to the primary question. The second point of order is 
that the Speakers’ rulings, and your rulings, in fact, are very clear that supplementary 
questions from the Government on Government questions should not be used to attack 
the Opposition. 
Mr SPEAKER : On the first —and I think it then relates to the second point of 
order—the supplementary question, i n my mind, was in order. There was no way I was 
to know what figures the Minister had had to take time to correct. So the question was 
definitely in order. As the answer has progressed, it is getting to a stage now when I 
could conclude that it has been de signed for no other purpose than to attack the Labour 
Opposition. I would be grateful if the Minister, if he wants to conclude his answer, 
would do so without further reference to Labour. 
Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN : Sure. In actual f act, of 10 practices in central 
Auckland nine are offering free doctors visits for under -13s. I accept Mrs King’s 
apology. I would like to table the transcript of a radio article entitled— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! No. Such transcripts are freely avai lable to all members if 
they so want them.  
Dairy Price—Impact on Wider Economy 
6. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of 
Finance: Does he agree with the Prime Minister that bad news about the New Zealand 
economy is overblown, and that while dairy prices are down, “95 percent of our 
economy is not involved in that”? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance): Yes. 
Grant Robertson : How does he reconcile his support for the Prime Minister’s 
statement with the following statement, also made by the Prime Minister: “When things 
are going well on our farms this flows through into the  small towns, the provincial

LAND TRANSPORT (SPEED LIMITS VALIDATION AND OTHER 
MATTERS) BILL 
First Reading 
Hon SIMON BRIDGES (Minister of Transport): I move, That the Land Transport 
(Speed Limits Validation and Other Matters) Bill be now read a first time.  This bill 
clarifies the power of local councils and other road -controlling authorities such as the 
New Zealand Transport Age ncy to set speed limits through their by -laws. The bill 
corrects some technical legal issues in the powers available to make some speed limit 
by-laws and the review process for local government by -laws. This bill ensures that 
these by -laws and the speed li mits made under them remain valid and therefore 
enforceable. The ability to set speed limits and enforce them is essential to public safety. 
Crashes on New Zealand roads claim lives, cause injuries, and devastate families and 
communities. Councils and othe r road -controlling authorities were always meant to 
have powers to set speed limit by-laws. This bill makes these requirements clear.  
Recent information has suggested that some road -controlling authorities may have 
made speed limit by -laws under powers th at may not have been available to them, or 
have omitted to comply fully with their bylaw -making powers conferred by local 
government Acts by not reviewing speed limit by -laws within the required time. In the 
interests of removing doubt and providing clarit y, this bill validates all speed limit by -
5134 Land Transport (Speed Limits Validation etc.) Bill 21 Jul 2015 
 
laws and confirms they were made correctly under appropriate legislation —either local 
government or land transport legislation. Although this bill addresses a potential 
problem with some speed limits set as far bac k as 2004, it is an urgent matter. Simply 
put, we cannot run the risk that some speed limits might be invalid while others are not. 
Passing this bill under urgency will prevent anyone from taking advantage of the speed 
limit validity question.  
The bill will make minor amendments to the Land Transport Act 1998, removing any 
doubt that road -controlling authorities can make speed limit by -laws under land 
transport legislation. This bill does not impact on speed limit by -laws made by airport 
authorities or Min isters of the Crown under legislation specific to them. Part 1 of the 
bill sets out what by -laws are covered by this amendment. Part 2 of the bill validates 
any by-laws and the speed limits made under them and the enforcement actions taken in 
relation to them.  
The bill also continues existing procedural requirements for certain by -law makers 
such as airport authorities, which are subject to separate legislation concerning their 
bylaw-making process. The bill also deems existing by -laws to have been made un der 
the Land Transport Act 1998. This will mean those by -laws originally made under local 
government legislation cease to be Local Government Act by -laws and will not be 
subject to the review requirements in the Local Government Act 2002.  
The bill, by validating speed limit by-laws, is retrospective. Retrospective legislation 
is rare, but in this case I believe it is necessary. I have inquired as to what other options 
exist to correct these matters. I can advise the House that there are no valid options. 
Although road-controlling authorities could make new speed limit by -laws, this would 
take some months to complete —a period during which many roads could have no valid 
speed limits other than 100 kilometres per hour. This creates, clearly, a public safety 
risk. I would not want police to be unable to enforce anything other than a 100 
kilometres per hour speed limit on our local streets. In addition, a road -controlling 
authority could not validate a previous by-law. This creates uncertainty as to the legality 
of enforcement actions. Therefore, we must move swiftly to protect public safety and 
provide certainty in this matter.  
This bill makes it clear that local councils will continue to be responsible for local 
decisions about speed limits, which should reflec t consultation and discussions with 
local communities. Local councils play an important role in road safety and are 
expected to work closely with other agencies such as Police and the New Zealand 
Transport Agency. Setting by-laws is therefore a function of local councils.  
We need to move swiftly to eliminate confusion. This bill makes it clear that these 
by-laws were as generally understood and were intended to be valid at all times, and 
that they remain so. No matter what causes a crash, speed directly af fects the force of 
impact and sometimes, of course, whether there is any impact at all. This means we 
cannot tolerate any ambiguity or uncertainty in the validity of speed limits. I commend 
this bill to the House.
