about some of the reasons why that is the case.  
The Minister has given us a bit of a thumbnail sketch of how this situation arose. The 
basic facts, I th ink, are these. Under Local Government Act 2002 councils were given 
the powers to set local speed limits in built -up areas and outside schools and so on, and, 
along with that power, councils were required to review those by -laws. I think, if my 
memory serves me correctly, the by-laws must be reviewed after 5 years and then every 
21 Jul 2015 Land Transport (Speed Limits Validation etc.) Bill 5135 
 
10 years thereafter. What has happened in this case is that the Kāpiti Coast District 
Council discovered in May this year that its speed limit by -law had been inadvertently 
revoked in 2012. That has obviously led to quite a bit of scurrying around by officials 
looking at how this happened, and it appears, we are advised, that there is a significant 
number of other councils who may find themselves in a similar situation. The upshot of  
all this is that it seems that there are tens of thousands —I do not think it is known 
exactly how many, but there could be tens of thousands—of speeding infringements that 
are technically invalid because of the failure of an unknown number of councils to 
follow the prescribed rules set down in the Local Government Act 2002. So that puts 
the Government in a very tricky position, and there are a whole lot of consequences that 
have to be considered as a result of that.  
Our view is that although retrospective  legislation is undesirable, mistakes do 
happen, and this is a pretty good example of mistakes happening on a fairly large scale. 
We believe that for reasons of public safety, for reasons of public confidence in our road 
safety system, of which speed limit s are obviously an essential part, and for fiscal and 
other practical reasons it is important that these mistakes are put right and that the laws 
and the speed limits that everybody has assumed have been in place over these years, 
and all of the infringements that were issued under these laws, are not overturned. That, 
I believe, would be untenable. It would be untenable for the communities that are 
protected by our road safety system and by speed limits. It would be untenable, I think, 
for the thousands of  New Zealanders who committed speeding infringements that they 
and everybody else assumed were valid.  
So let us talk a little bit more about some of the detail. The background to this is that 
there is the Land Transport Rule: Setting of Speed Limits 2003,  otherwise known as the 
speed limits rule. It basically sets a default 100 -kilometre-an-hour speed limit for all 
roads, unless this has been reduced by the relevant authority, like a council. Then, under 
that, local councils all around the country have the  power to set local speed limits, and I 
think that that is as it should be. It is an entirely appropriate thing for local communities 
to have that power. But the Local Government Act 2002 does require that the by -laws 
setting those speed limits are reviewe d—first, after 5 years, and then every 10 years 
after that.  
What the solution that this bill brings to the House does is it sets out to validate speed 
limits that have been created since 2004, regardless of whether they were promulgated 
under potentially invalid by-laws. I repeat: as far as I have been advised, it is unclear 
about the possible scale of this problem. I think we know with certainty that the Kāpiti 
Coast District Council has put its hand up and said that that is the case, but there may 
well be potentially quite a large number of others. It also validates enforcement actions 
that have been carried out in relation to those by-laws since 2004.  
What the bill does is it removes any ambiguity, or it attempts to clarify the powers in 
the Land Transport Act 1998 for road-controlling authorities like the councils to make a 
speed limit by-law, and then it clarifies the procedural requirements for those authorities 
around that power to make by -laws. My understanding of the bill —I have not had a 
chance to go through the bill in detail yet —is that although it leaves those powers and 
those responsibilities with the councils, it removes the requirement to review them 
every 5 years and 10 years, which is the thing that has got councils into this mess in the 
first place.  
What is the case for urgency? Why should this legislation be pushed through all 
stages this afternoon? Let me just touch on those. There is clearly a risk to road safety, 
to the safety of communities throughout the country, if there is any kind  of confusion or 
perception that the speed limits that everyone has thought are in place are suddenly 
thought to not apply or are unenforceable. Where the New Zealand Police has enforced 
5136 Land Transport (Speed Limits Validation etc.) Bill 21 Jul 2015 
 
invalid speed limits over the last few years, that obviously sets off  a whole chain of 
consequences: demerit points, fines, other sanctions, licences lost, and so on. If this bill 
was not passed with urgency, the people who experienced those sanctions could then 
argue that they have unlawfully suffered the consequences. I t hink that it would create a 
situation of real confusion, including significant financial risk to the Government, if all 
of those infringements and the penalties that followed from them were called into 
question, not to mention the possibility of individual s seeking compensation for loss of 
employment, disqualification, or even, in some cases, imprisonment.  
The fourth point that I would raise is that it would put our police force, which is out 
there every day on the roads around New Zealand trying to keep t he roads safe, 
protecting people, and enforcing the speed limits, in a very, very invidious position. It 
would undermine confidence in the police but also in the entire road safety system.  
I want to make the point that although, again, I think none of us feels great about 
passing retrospective legislation, the Legislation Advisory Committee has noted that 
retrospective legislation can be justified in some circumstances. It quotes, for example, 
bills to “validate matters that were generally understood and i ntended to be lawful, but 
were in fact unlawful as a result of a technical error;”, or, secondly, to “address a matter 
that is essential to public safety;”. I think it is fair to say that this bill ticks both the 
boxes in the guidelines that are set out by the Legislation Advisory Committee.

including during the Committee stage, when we will be able to, hopefully, tease out 
more detail about this bill. Thank you.

Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Green): I rise on behalf of the Green Party to speak to the

Wellington we have got some lower speed limits. On Waiheke Island, where I used to 
live, we lowered the speed limit there fro m 100 to 80 on the main straight —it was 
incredible that it was ever 100 kilometres an hour on such a small island. In the process, 
by lowering those speed limits, we have undoubtedly saved many lives and many 
injuries—the lives of not only motorists, who m ay have been going fast and if they had 
an accident then they would have got hurt more severely if they had been going faster,

legislation does, effectively, is validate the work local governments have been doing to 
set all of those speed limits, because otherwise —they are meant to be reviewed every 5 
years, and clearly some of them have not been—all of those lower speed limits less than

until now would almost certainly be challengeable in court. So it is essential that we 
introduce this legislation.  
Of course, there are a lot of things that you could do under urgency in the transport

law and if I follow the rules I can’t be prosecuted by the State.” So the danger of

may use clever politics, but it has no plans to address our long -term challenges facing 
New Zealand. It promised a Budget surplus and on Budget day it did not deliver on that 
promise. 
We believe that every New Zealander should be entitled to access quality public 
education of the highest standard thr oughout their entire lives. Quality education 
ensures that every Kiwi, regardless of who they are, where they come from, and 
whether or not they are rich or poor, can achieve their full potential to contribute to our 
society and our economy. 
This Governmen t claims, as we have just heard from the Minister for Tertiary 
Education, Skills and Employment, that changes to tertiary education are providing 
results. It is great for people to get qualifications, and we expect to see constant changes 
and improvements over the years in this particular area, but what we are also seeing is 
universities and polytechnics being required to do so much more with much less money. 
National has been underfunding the tertiary education sector for far too long, and the 
cracks are beginning to show. 
On Budget day it was announced —as we heard the chair of the Education and 
Science Committee address before —that there is $130 million worth of operating 
funding over the next 4 years for tertiary education. But when the tertiary education  
Minister was questioned about this when he came to the select committee, he conceded 
that only $7 million of this funding was actually new money. The rest of the balance 
was made up of reallocations, and it is not new funding at all. That is not being str aight-
up with New Zealanders. 
New Zealand now ranks close to the bottom of the OECD on tertiary education 
spending per student. We are behind Australia, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, 
Germany, and a few other countries. We are well below the OECD averag e. Under this 
Government the total spending on tertiary education has fallen from $3.194 billion in 
2009 to $3 billion in 2015. We need further investment in tertiary education, not radical 
restructuring to align our universities and our polytechnics with the Government’s 
corporate view of the world in which it interferes with academic freedom, democracy, 
and independence.  
Under this Government we have around 70,000 young New Zealanders who are not 
in employment, education, or training—or the “neet” numbers. This number is just way 
too high. It is not acceptable. Under this Government, 40 percent of our total 
unemployed are young people. Again, it is just unacceptable. This is the highest 
percentage of total unemployment of any youth population whatsoever i n the OECD 
countries. I do not know about you, Mr Chairperson, but I think that this statistic is 
really quite shameful for a country like New Zealand. We have one of the best 
educational systems in the world, and yet we have 40 percent of our total unempl oyed 
being young people. This surely is something that must be addressed. This Government 
is focused on the 1,600 or so 16 to 17-year-olds, but I think that this focus is wrong. The 
focus should instead be on the 70,000 or so young people who are currently  not in 
employment, education, or training. 
The safety of our children should be paramount and it should be the main objective 
when the Government considers funding for school buses, not cutting costs. So buried 
in the details of this year’s Budget is $90 million worth of funding cuts for school 
transport. We remember the horror ride for Green Bay High School students one 
afternoon when they had a relief driver. The safety of our children when riding in school

buses should definitely not be one of those thi ngs that the Government looks at in terms 
of cost-cutting. I do not know of any parent —not one—who would want their children 
to experience or to go through a similar traumatic experience like the one that these 
Green Bay students went through because of this Government’s cost-cutting measures.

Hon NIKKI KAYE (Associate Minister of Education): I am very pleased to speak. 
That speech from Tracey Martin was a load of rubbish. I normally rate that member 
very highly, but the facts are these: under our Governme nt for the last 6 years we have 
successively increased the education budget —$10.8 billion in the most difficult 
financial times. Every single year we have increased the education budget. Secondly, 
when it comes to our most vulnerable students, whether that  is students who have 
special education difficulties or whether that is those students who have had real issues 
in terms of numeracy and literacy, this Budget is better than ever for them. 
Let us walk through it. If we look at early childhood education par ticipation, 
particularly around Māori and Pacific young people, that is up. That is up by 4 to 5 
percent. That is incredibly significant, and that is about the future of our country. When 
we actually look at the facts in terms of participation around early  childhood education, 
we are absolutely on track for 98 percent. We have got more money going into early 
childhood education—I think there is $75 million in this Budget. That is about doing 
everything we can to make sure that all students in this country are successful. 
When it comes to special education, this Budget is great in terms of special 
education. We have got $40 million going into ongoing resourcing scheme funding. 
That means that for the 500 young people who have and need that additional support,  
whether that is teacher -aide time, whether that is physiotherapy, or whether that is 
speech language therapy, we are putting the resource into them. 
I want to acknowledge the Hon Hekia Parata. I think this is a great Budget in terms 
of what she has done. She has real vision, and she is investing in some of our most 
vulnerable students. The Budget also includes $24 million for additional class support. 
That is 1,500 —that is the first phase of another group of students who need that 
additional help in terms of our education system. So when that member tells us that 
somehow we have underfunded education, well, it is a 26 percent increase in special 
education. Under our Government there is $500 million more for some of our most 
vulnerable students. 
When it come s to trade academies there is more money than ever. So when that 
member says that we are not aspirational for Northland, that is a complete load of 
rubbish. What are we doing in terms of modern learning and education environments 
for Northland? Well, the o ther day I found out that we are so far ahead of schedule in 
terms of the roll out of Network for Learning —that is fast, uncapped data paid for by

the Crown; a real passport to the future for these students —that 600,000 students are

been in Government. 
CATHERINE DELAHUNTY (Green): Tēnā koe, Mr Chair. Kia ora tātou katoa. It 
is great to take a call on education because I do not believe that there is anyone in the 
Education and Science Committee who is not interested and concerned about aspects of 
education. Often members of the publ ic say to us: why do you not all put aside your 
differences and just work together? But I think, listening to the debate tonight, there are 
some underlying themes that make it clear why we do not always agree. One of those is 
the pedagogical vision of what education is for, and I think we have heard very strongly 
from the Government that it is aspirational, in its terms, for education and that the 
purpose of education is to serve the economy. 
That is not the view of the Green Party. The Green Party believes  that education is a 
whole lot more than serving the economy and that, in fact, the economy should serve its 
people. Education is about lifelong learning for all people, and it is not about —with due 
respect to the chair of the Education and Science Committ ee, Dr Jian Yang —getting 
them into education earlier for longer. It is actually about acknowledging that education 
needs to be of quality and that the goal of education is equity. That is a very different 
pedagogical goal, and that is why we have problems with the Government’s obsession 
with targets and assessment, which is an educational model that is reductionist and 
unsuccessful in other countries. 
The current education estimates and the Minister at the select committee were all 
about targets, targets, t argets. Why is that a problem? It is a problem because the early 
5180 Estimates Debate 21 Jul 2015 
 
childhood education sector may be about to reach 96 percent to 98 percent participation, 
but when I asked the chief executive of the ministry about quality, he said: “That will 
come later. We are going to get participation first and then we will find a way to figure 
out how to improve quality.” So what in fact we have got is a huge push, including 
through the Work and Income system, to make parents place their children under the 
age of 5 into early childhood education, but quality has not yet been sorted out, people. 
So how comfortable do we feel about making sure that our little children are all getting 
this brilliant start in life, when there is no commitment to quality? 
Therefore, we have go t the whole spectrum in early childhood education from the 
absolutely inspiring and wonderful—often smaller in number, high -ratio trained teacher 
centres plus the kōhanga and playcentre, where they have succeeded in holding on to 
fantastic whānau engagement, which is increasingly hard in this economy—and then we 
have got the opposite, which are basically baby barns, where people who do not have a 
choice because they have no public transport and no resources are forced to use the 
baby barn down the road, the  large franchise, the commercial model. So the education 
sector is torn between a genuine commitment to learning, because it enhances our 
humanity as well as our society as well as our economy, and making sure we meet 
targets. 
This Government has pushed th is right through to national standards and through to 
the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA). So national standards —
again, another one of those measurables that actually does not deal with the 
unmeasurable, which is children, because ch ildren all learn at different rates. We have 
this system with NCEA as well, where we are claiming we are going to get to the target 
of 80 percent achieving level 2, but again questions are being asked by academics about 
whether we have lowered standards in  order to meet the target; what the real quality is 
of what is happening in our secondary schools. 
So if we are concerned about public quality education, it is not enough to spout the 
numbers and talk the rhetoric. It is absolutely not enough. We actually have to know 
whether early childhood education is of quality, because the most important years that 
we pay lip service to are our small children. We have to know that kids are getting lunch 
as well as breakfast, which is where the Green Party has stood str ong on feeding 
children properly, and not saying that if charities and the Government want to have a bit 
of a partnership and have breakfast, that is OK; they do not need lunch. Well, of course 
if we lifted wages and had a decent economy, then the parents could afford it, but right 
now, as was shown in the House today in our question on inequality, we have a long 
way to go on that, so we still need to feed our children in schools. That is why we need 
a decent school lunch programme. 
Honestly, there are some inspiring programmes that schools are leading, but they are 
paying for it themselves in many instances. Sometimes teachers are paying for it, 
sometimes communities have stepped up, but there is no consistency and there is a real 
need for a decent, State -supported lunch programme that is flexible and school and 
community-led. 
Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Labour —New Lynn): It is a pleasure to take a second 
brief call in this debate and to focu s on education issues, where once again we see that 
we have a Government that is long on promises, long on rhetoric, and not delivering in 
the reality. Let us take members opposite at their word. I think all parents care for 
nothing more than the well -being of their children, and I believe members opposite are 
sincere in their wish to see our children succeed. The question is whether the 
programme that they are enacting is going to deliver on that promise. 
Let us first look at the compulsory education secto r and then at the tertiary sector. 
The Government has been known for two great changes to compulsory education: 
21 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5181 
 
national standards and charter schools. National standards have been panned around the 
world. They cause people to teach to the test. They are t he exact opposite of what a 
modern millennial economy demands, which is that you can get basic education off the 
internet but you need to learn to think critically. That is why teaching to the test —one-
size-fits-all, absolute achievement rather than relati ve improvement —is a road to 
pedagogical nowhere. In my electorate, where 40 percent of my constituents were not 
born in New Zealand —and for many, many students English is not a first language —
having an English -based national standards, even if it were obje ctive, even if it were 
specific, even if it were moderated objectively, which it is not, would make no sense at 
all. The Government is taking education backwards. 
The second great proposal of this Government is charter schools, and charter schools 
make no sense. More money is given per student by miles, but the school does not have 
to teach the curriculum, the teachers do not have to be licensed, they are not subject to 
the Official Information Act, and in many cases the contracts the Government has 
entered into are so brain -dead that the assets are not even secured. For example, a 
Whangarei charter school has $2.5 million in taxpayer funding unaccounted for. 
Another Auckland charter school was guaranteed funding for 160 places but maxed out 
at 120 with, as far as I am aware, no recovery. More and more costs are being passed to 
parents, and too many parents cannot afford them because of the rapidly growing 
inequalities in our society. If a kid is hungry he or she cannot learn. Let us feed our kids, 
let us give them a decent start, and let us have an education system that actually teaches 
what kids are going to need in this 21st century. 
Then we go on to tertiary education, and here once again the Government is, sadly, 
not being straight with New Zealanders. Fr om the Minister’s own lips, as recorded in 
the report of the Education and Science Committee, there was no $113 million “further 
funding” for education. By the Minister’s own admission there was only $7 million, and 
that is gross of an increased tax take f rom the Inland Revenue Department, which 
actually makes it negative. But even if it were $7 million, that is a massive real -terms 
cut to tertiary education. The tertiary system is underfunded. It has a micro -managing 
Minister who lacks the credibility to get the funding, and he lacks the plan to deliver it. 
The institutions in this sector are a mess. This Government removed the strategy and 
policy function from the Tertiary Education Commission. It now says it just 
operationalises things. Where has the stra tegy function gone? It is not found in the 
Ministry of Education—it is focused on the compulsory sector. In reality, what there is 
sits in the Ministry of —wait for it —Business, Innovation and Employment. That is, as 
others have said, a reductionist view of  education and one that is patently not working. 
For the individual student, pathways are not there to the jobs of the future. Why not? 
Because the funding cuts are biting. 
The Government has put an arbitrary 7 -year limit on student loans —the famous “7 
EFTS” policy, which means that even 40 percent of medical students cannot get funding 
for their last 1 or 2 years of study. For other recognised long degrees —double degrees 
or doctoral courses—the loans run out before the degree is awarded. That might be fine  
if you are a silver spoon brigade kid, but if you are an average kid from an average 
family, our country and you will be the poorer.
